newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Mir crew rests, repairs delayed.
newsitem.headline: Russian Mir crew rests, repairs delayed.

text.p: The crew of Russia's damaged Mir space station, back in control of their craft after a self-inflicted energy supply crisis, were given a day of rest on Saturday, officials said.
An official from U.S. space agency said NASA that Russians Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin and American Michael Foale would only do some minor repairs during the day.

"They will be spending most of time resting except they are working on two gyrodynes," Kathlene Maliga told reporters at the Mission Control outside Moscow referring to devices that keep Mir's solar panels angled towards the sun.

The station's 12 gyrodynes went off and the crippled craft briefly lost orientation when one of the crew -- officials will not say who -- pulled out a cable, causing a vital computer to crash on Thursday.
Maliga said the crew restarted seven gyrodynes out of 12 on board on Friday and were working on two more on Saturday.

It takes eight or nine gyrodynes, which use no fuel at all, to maintain the orientation of the panels, she added. After the computer crash the the panels were being held in alignment by electronically controlled motors.
A spokesman for the mission Control said that the power supply to the station has been resumed.
"The situation on board is normal and the energy has been fully re-supplied," Vladislav Tachilo said.

The computer mishap added to the latest string of misfortunes haunting the crew of the ageing space laboratory which had started when a Progress cargo craft holed the Spektr scientific module on June 25 during a training docking.

The incident, which deprived the station of nearly half its energy resources, was followed by a mysterious leak of unidentified liquid and the news that Tsibliyev had experienced irregular heartbeats.

Experts on earth, who have held consultations after the latest incident which they attribute to a human error, appear to have decided that the main repairs on board will be carried out by the next crew due to reach Mir on August 7.
Mission director Vladimir Solovyov told reporters that the cosmonauts were advised during a video link on Saturday that their task was limited to preparing the way for subsequent repair work.
But the final decision on the future plans, he added, was still to be taken by a meeting of senior officials at the Mission Control planned for Monday.
Two fresh Russian cosmonauts, Pavel Vinogradov and Anatoly Solovyov, are already in training at Star City near Moscow for the dangerous job of entering the airless Spektr module.
They will have to mend cables cut after the June 25 accident and make a spacewalk to patch the puncture.
Tsibliyev and Lazutkin had planned to return to earth on August 26, but Solovyov said they would leave the station a little earlier than planned. He did not say when exactly.
He said British-born NASA physicist Foale would go home as planned aboard a U.S. Shuttle in September.
Maliga said Foale would continue some of his planned research on Sunday, including greenhouse experiments.
